Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.explanation: The Threat items describe a chronic interpersonal/home-intrusion danger template (monitoring for someone entering the home, planning escape routes, feeling unsafe specifically at night), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item about listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal/intrusion danger theme that is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma type of natural disaster. For a natural-disaster profile, loud sounds and generalized hypervigilance are plausible, but specifically monitoring for a person entering the home suggests a different trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: The appraisal that institutions failed to protect him is possible after a disaster, but in combination with the home-intrusion threat cue it contributes to a mixed interpersonal-threat profile rather than a coherent natural-disaster formulation. The rest of the profile centers on terror, overwhelm, and disorganized memory, so this item is questionable mainly because it pulls toward a different trauma narrative when paired with the flagged threat item.

vignette:
Daniel Mercer was 45 when a massive tornado tore through the county where he was working as a military medic on temporary domestic emergency support. He had spent years moving toward danger in a controlled way, in uniform, with training, protocols, and a clear role. That day unraveled every assumption he had relied on. He remembered the sky turning an unnatural green-gray and the sound arriving before he fully understood what he was hearing, a deep mechanical roar mixed with splintering wood, metal wrenching apart, car alarms, and people shouting over one another. He had been moving toward a collapsed residential block with medical gear when the wind shifted hard enough to throw debris across the road. In fragments, he remembered seeing a roof peel away, a truck rolled onto its side, and a child’s bicycle lodged high in a tree. He knew there were injured people around him and that he kept trying to orient himself, but when he spoke about the day now, the sequence came out broken and uncertain. He would start with pulling a man from wreckage, then jump to the sound of glass exploding, then to kneeling in mud with blood on his gloves, unable to say what came first. What remained intact was not chronology but terror. When the memory returned, it did not feel like something over. It felt as if the same force were bearing down again, and he would become so flooded that he had to stop talking.

In the months after the tornado, Daniel returned to work, but the world no longer felt governed by anything dependable. He had once believed that preparation mattered, that skill and discipline could create order even in crisis. Now he was certain those beliefs had been naive. A clear morning no longer meant safety; sturdy buildings no longer looked sturdy; ordinary life no longer seemed to rest on anything solid. He found himself watching the environment constantly, scanning windows, doors, tree movement, the quality of the light outside. Loud or unexpected sounds hit him with immediate force. A slammed locker in the medical unit, a supply cart crashing over a threshold, a helicopter passing low, even a dropped metal tray could jolt him upright before he had time to think. In those moments his whole body was braced, his attention narrowed, and he stayed keyed up long afterward. Colleagues noticed that he positioned himself near exits during briefings and turned toward every noise in the room. Even at home, in the house he had shared with his wife before she died, he could not settle into the furniture or rest through an evening. He would tell himself he was safe in his own living room and still feel unable to relax, as if letting his guard down would be a mistake.

The sensory pieces of the disaster were especially potent. Wind rattling the windows or the sudden groan of the house in bad weather could stop him cold. He did not experience these sounds as minor reminders; they carried the same charge as the day of the tornado. He would become tense and silent, listening hard, tracking every creak in the walls. At work, when storm warnings came through or weather reports played in the background of the break room television, he lingered in a state of readiness that he could not switch off. The setting of his job made this difficult to escape. Emergency medicine meant alarms, shouted communication, rolling equipment, and abrupt movement, all of which kept him feeling watchful and overprepared. He still performed his duties, but the effort of staying composed around noise and unpredictability was exhausting, and he had begun turning down optional shifts and stepping out of common areas when activity built up around him.

His relationship to himself had changed just as starkly. Daniel described feeling as though he no longer recognized the man moving through his life. For most of his adulthood, being a medic had given him a stable sense of identity: capable, useful, steady under pressure. Since the tornado, those words no longer fit in any reassuring way. He could not make the event sit inside the older story he had about himself or the world. What frightened him was not only what had happened that day but what it seemed to prove—that life could be smashed apart without warning and without reason, and that the values he had built himself around no longer held. Since becoming widowed he had already been living with loss; after the tornado, loss felt less like one chapter of his life and more like the shape of reality itself. He found himself going through routines without conviction. Nothing felt meaningful in the way it once had. Work, meals, household tasks, conversations with friends from the service all seemed flattened, as if he were participating from a distance.

He sought help only after realizing that this was not easing with time. During a recent storm, thunder cracked unexpectedly while he was in the garage, and he reacted so strongly that he dropped what he was carrying and stood frozen, heart pounding, unable to think past the sound. Later, trying to explain it, he became overwhelmed and had to stop midsentence because the terror of the tornado was suddenly back in the room with him. That moment unsettled him enough to come in. He said he was tired of living in a state of constant guard and tired of feeling like his life had been emptied out. What he fears most is that the world is exactly as unstable as it now seems and that the person he used to be is gone for good. What he hopes, though cautiously, is that he might someday hear the wind or a slammed door and remain in the present, and that some part of his life might feel real and worth inhabiting again.
